extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry; critics and readers learning practical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for close reading and critical evaluation of poems, emphasizing the interaction of metrical form, sense, feeling, and the reader's responses. Aimed at improving classroom and private practice in practical criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to poetic form (movement of words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Half perhaps of the feeling that poetry carries comes through its form (and through the interaction of form and content); many readers do not understand the importance that attaches to the movement of words in verse nor have just ideas of how to seize this movement or judge it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form and the movement of words are essential to poetic feeling; educational methods should teach readers to grasp this movement (see numerous protocol examples cited: 1.161, 3.15, 3.51, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate metrical excellence with strict regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion that regularity is the merit of verse is a damaging protocol; no set of rules has been found that makes metrical excellence identical with regular conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than strict conformity, an arrangement of departures from and returns to the pattern often yields rhythmical interest; insistence on regularity produces mechanical reading and other harms (see 13.62, 3.44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate rhythm with sense and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between good rhythm and bad is not simply a difference between certain sequences of sounds; it goes deeper, and to understand it we have to take note of the meanings of the words as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhythm admired in verse is largely a rhythm of the mental activity through which we apprehend sound and sense together—so evaluate rhythm in conjunction with a poem's sense and feeling (examples: reader responses to Poem 4; projection phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat inherent sound as an important but subordinate factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual sounds (the skeleton) are a very important contributing factor though they do not carry the whole responsibility for the rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the 'skeleton' of sound is too much out of joint relative to sense and feeling, no depth of realisation will overcome the disability—changing the rhythm while preserving vocabulary illustrates this (example transformation of Hamlet line produces comic-opera effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metrical pattern as a convenience, not an obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no obligation upon verses to conform to any standard; the pattern is only a convenience—an invaluable one—but it has no compulsory powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pattern indicates general movement and gives a model or central line from which variations gain significance; it supplies orientation but must not be enforced as a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical scansion and ruthless lopping of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical reading—the 'cruel forcing' of syllables into a mould and the ruthless lopping away of vocables—is fatal to the movement of the verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such treatment stems from misapplied classical training and damages the poem's life (cf. 3.44, 8.44, 12.51, 13.62).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat poetic rhythm as independent of sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion that poetic rhythm is independent of sense is hurtful; rhythm we ascribe to words is influenced by our apprehension of their meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare phrases with similar inherent sounds but different meanings (Deep into a gloomy grot vs Peep into a roomy cot) to see how meaning changes the ascribed rhythm; scanning must take meaning into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize projection in the perception of sound and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: The mysterious glory which seems to inhere in the sound of certain lines is a projection of the thought and emotion they evoke; we ascribe rhythm to sound because of mental adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that what listeners detect in performance may be signs of the reader's understanding rather than inherent sonic superiority; this affects how we judge recorded readings or foreign-language listening experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test claims of independent sonic virtue with dummy/nonsense verse
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mere sound of verse possessed independent aesthetic virtue, one could compose nonsense syllables approximating a masterpiece and retain similar virtue — experiments with dummy verse show this is not persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to replicate poetic virtue with nonsense reveal the interplay of sense and sound; inability to recover the poem's effect suggests meaning is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate form and meaning together as the secret of Style
rubrics_metrics.description: The close co-operation of the form with the meaning—modifying it and being modified by it—is the chief secret of Style in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language that extirpates matter in the form or elevates form above content; look for subtle, intelligible ways form and meaning alter one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define bad reading as that which prevents entry into the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad reading is reading that prevents the reader himself from entering into the poem rather than merely offending listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projection and self-deception in reading often make readers think they have given suitable rhythms when they have not; aim for readings that genuinely allow the poem to disclose itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer slow private reading when form is unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: We are more likely to read too fast than to read too slow; a very slow private reading gives a better chance for the necessary interaction of form and meaning to develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private reading aloud is recommended as an aid in working out form; public reading (especially in classroom) should be discouraged until the poem has yielded many of its secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of poor recordings and public performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Very unfortunately most of the gramophone records yet available must be described as exceedingly bad in both senses; they would justify in a sensitive child a permanent aversion from poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad public or recorded performances can instill irreversible habits of sentimentalisation, exaggeration, or aversion; teachers should select good models and caution students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat imagery cautiously — distinguish personal vividness from poetic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem which calls up a 'beautiful picture' is not thereby proved to be a good poem; the detail of most readers' imagery is likely to be irrelevant and dependent on circumstances accidental to the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualisers are especially exposed to this danger; consider whether imagery genuinely embodies the poem's meaning before using it as evidence of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check the relevance of associations and memories
rubrics_metrics.description: When associations (memories or trains of thought) intrude, we must ask whether they really spring from the meaning or are accidental by-products of a reading that does not realise the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the association has an essential bond with the poem and whether accidents of mood, history, or temperament have twisted it; examples include personal reminiscences and trains of thought noted in protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparisons with care — avoid superficial class-based judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons are useful only when they can be traced deeper; direct comparisons based on superficial classification (cloud poems, sonnets, etc.) can only serve to exhibit stupid reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great services of comparison come when they assist closer reading; never judge a poem merely by likeness to an external class without exploring real commonalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting personal obsessions (hobby-horses) dominate reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The intrusion into the poem of the hobby-horse or the obsession (indignant moralist, educational reformer, symbolist, etc.) leads to flagrant irrelevance and distorts judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for readers who substitute their preoccupations for the poem itself (examples: 6.36–6.38, 12.11, 8.41, 10.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow personal memories only when genuine, relevant, and respectful of the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Memories and personal situations inevitably affect reading and can be legitimate; the only conditions are that they must be genuine and relevant, and must respect the liberty and autonomy of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such memories can serve as a touchstone for reality and are sometimes indispensable in judging accuracy and verisimilitude (examples in discussion of Poem 9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize stock responses and assess their utility versus danger
rubrics_metrics.description: A stock response is a ready-made habitual reaction that may be convenient and necessary in many life situations but can be disadvantageous in reading poetry when it prevents a more appropriate, specific response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey whether a response is a misfit introduced by habit (e.g., stock epithet usage, stock images) and consider means of avoiding harmful stock responses; examples include barriers to Poem 2, political or religious prejudices affecting readings (7.2, 9.14–9.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conscious that interpretation is driven by active interests
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person misreads a poem it is because, as he is at that moment, he wants to—the interpretation he puts upon the words is the most agile and active among several possibilities; every interpretation is motivated by some interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should be wary of initial prepossession or desire for approval/condemnation which can seize the interpretive process; cultivate a 'major interest' of faithful reading to control local biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing stock rhythm that distorts the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: A stock rhythm can be imported as easily as a stock idea and may distort a passage whose adequate reading develops otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readers habitually apply conventional prosodic patterns, they may miss a poem's particular movement (see examples cited such as 8.41 and 3.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge a poem by standards external to itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligent critics should realise that no poem can be judged by standards external to itself; applying external standards (expectation that poems in the same class must be alike) leads to stupid reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poems on their own internal aims and structures rather than by comparison to an external ideal or genre stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify impersonality and native familiarity as signs of stock-response poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems whose mental movements are few and simple, whose phrasing is extremely impersonal and whose movements are native familiarity rather than acquired familiarity, often indicate composition from stock responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such poems may lack individual character and personal twist (contrast with Donne's Sonnet); their facility and ease may explain immunity from serious misunderstanding but also reveal their stock nature.
